Read our Privacy notice A prison officer has been jailed for eight months after engaging in an inappropriate relationship with a drug dealer who styled himself as the "Latvian Pablo Escobar". Jahvine Kwamba, 21, was working at HMP Fosse Way in Leicestershire when she began a relationship with prisoner Roberts Sokolovs. Leicester Crown Court heard that Kwamba initiated contact with Sokolovs 1,367 times while he was held at the category C prison between 24 February and 3 June 2024. Sokolovs, who was imprisoned in 2022 for his involvement in the "Jimmy Line" county lines drug ring operating between Skelmersdale, Lancashire, and Lincoln, was later transferred to an immigration removal centre at Gatwick Airport in June 2024. Prosecution counsel Rawaid Javed told the court that sexually explicit photographs and messages were exchanged between the pair on Snapchat after this transfer. The court heard that there were 5,441 contacts between Kwamba and Sokolovs on Snapchat while he was at HMP Fosse Way, and a further 4,211 contacts while he was at the removal centre. open image in gallery Kwamba hides her face as she arrives at court ( PA ) Kwamba denies any physical sexual contact, a claim the prosecution stated it was "sceptical" about. Sokolovs was deported to Latvia in November 2024 and was never interviewed regarding the relationship. Kwamba, from Doncaster, South Yorkshire, was arrested in July 2024 and had previously pleaded guilty to two counts of misconduct in a public office. The court also heard details of financial transactions. Kwamba received five payments totalling £1,495 from Sokolovs’s mother, Zita Sokolova, 53, between 18 March and 2 July 2024. Additionally, 18 payments totalling £4,665 were sent to her by his 20-year-old sister, Venera Sokolova, during the same period. Kwamba, in turn, sent seven payments totalling £660 to Sokolovs’s sister between 27 March and 1 July 2024. Mr Javed noted there were "no obvious patterns" to these transactions, and Kwamba spent an initial £500 payment from Zita Sokolova on food and clothing. Sam Ponniah, defending Kwamba, who was 19 at the time of the offences, argued she had shown "significant levels of naivety and immaturity" and had been "well in over her head". He highlighted that she had been a prison officer for only four months and was in charge of 64 prisoners, away from home in an unfamiliar area. open image in gallery Kwamba was sentenced at Leicester Crown Court ( PA ) Mr Ponniah stated: "She has real and substantiated remorse for her actions, it is clear from her letter that one of the things that weighs heavily on her is ruining a job she thought she was doing well at… she knows she has thrown that all away." Kwamba now works at a car rental company. Sokolovs’s mother and sister, both from Skelmersdale, also faced charges. They had previously pleaded guilty to transmitting or causing the transmission of an image by electronic communications from inside HMP Fosse Way between 24 February and 3 June 2024. The hearing revealed Venera Sokolova contacted her brother 191 times while he was in prison, and his mother 33 times. In a voluntary police interview in November 2024, Zita Sokolova admitted sending her son money in prison and said her son told her Kwamba was going to "help him". Venera Sokolova stated she knew Kwamba as her brother’s girlfriend but was unaware she was a prison officer, having been asked by her brother to contact her. Jonathan Dunne, defending the Sokolovas, argued that "when women of good character come before the courts, there is invariably a man behind it." He maintained they did not realise Kwamba was a prison officer, believing her to be merely his girlfriend. Mr Dunne added: "If one looks at the reality, (Roberts Sokolovs) is a county lines drug dealer and the women are being told to send money in. It won’t be the first time women have done things men have asked them to do out of a sense of loyalty, a sense of fear." Zita Sokolova received a four-month prison sentence, suspended for one year, and was ordered to pay £400 costs. Venera Sokolova was given a 12-month community order with a requirement to attend 15 probation appointments. open image in gallery Sokolovs styled himself on the infamous Pablo Escobar ( AFP/Getty ) Addressing all three defendants, Judge Timothy Spencer KC said: "This case strikes at the heart of any functioning criminal justice system, including a functioning prison system, where those running a prison can have some confidence that discipline and good order is maintained and not continually undermined. “You, in your different ways, have all contributed to the undermining of that system of law and order and each of you have struck at the heart of the maintenance of law and order in this country." Sentencing Kwamba, who covered her face upon entering court, the judge noted her extensive training and the importance of maintaining integrity. He said: "You knew from the start that any money at all, let alone over £6,000, was exposing you to the same sort of risk I identified and that the transfer of any amount was utterly wrong." Judge Spencer suspected Kwamba was "pretty lonely and vulnerable", adding: "You were easy prey and easy pickings for Roberts, who obviously decided he could exploit you." He concluded that it was a "tragedy you have thrown it all away." To the Sokolovas, Judge Spencer warned: "If you ever had any illusions about how serious this is, those illusions have been dispelled today. What you did was extremely serious. Allowing illicit phone contact with a prisoner is fundamentally wrong. You must have known you were contributing to that but you will both go home tonight. You could not have come closer to following (Kwamba) through the door." He added that Zita, being older, "should have known better," while Venera, who was very young at the time, had "done a lot of growing up" and should not waste this chance. https://www.express.co.uk/news/royal/225.text: Home News Royal The Duchess of Edinburgh's first title had a unique story behind it (Image: Getty) The Duchess of Edinburgh is often declared to be one of the safest pairs of hands the monarchy has, but she could have had an entirely different role if history had followed a different course after a surprising request was sent to Prince Edward in 1994. At the time, Estonia was undergoing significant political changes, which led it to ask Queen Elizabeth's youngest son, Prince Edward, to become its head of state. Buckingham Palace politely declined the "charming" but unusual offer. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT However, if Prince Edward had accepted, it would have drastically altered subsequent events. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1994, several new countries emerged in Eastern Europe, including Estonia. During Estonia's first elections, the Independent Royalist Party, which wanted the country to be a monarchy, won eight seats in Parliament and began searching for a suitable candidate for the top job. The Sunday Telegraph reported at the time that the party leader had written to the Royal Family to ask if Prince Edward would consider becoming their king, as they believed he was "perfect" for the role. The country expressed its honour and admiration for Prince Edward, inviting him to accept a unique offer because they "enormously" admired him. Buckingham Palace reportedly responded to the peculiar proposal, stating it was "a charming idea but a rather unlikely one". Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Prince Edward and Sophie have been married since 1999 (Image: Getty) Prince Philip wished for his title to be passed to his youngest son and his wife (Image: Getty) In 2023, Prince Edward and his wife Sophie experienced a significant change in their royal status, becoming the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, a title with profound meaning, especially for Sophie. The previous Duchess of Edinburgh was the late Queen, who held the title from her marriage in 1947 until her accession in 1952. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Sophie shared a very close relationship with the late Queen and recalled the moment Prince Philip expressed his wish for them to take on the Edinburgh title. She said in a previous interview: "We sat there slightly stunned. He literally came straight in and said, 'Right. I'd like it very much if you would consider that." However, this wasn't the only title option for the couple; before their 1999 wedding, it was announced that they would be known as the Earl and Countess of Wessex, which surprised many, as it was expected that Edward would receive a dukedom like his brothers. Opting for the title of Earl made Prince Edward the first royal since the Tudor era to break with convention. The decision wasn't a snub towards the Queen; rather, it was at Edward's behest to hold the distinct title of Earl of Wessex – a title dormant since the 11th century. Influenced by his fondness for the movie 'Shakespeare in Love', featuring a character named Lord Wessex, Edward reportedly expressed his preference during a conversation with the Queen. A royal insider revealed in 2010, "He liked the sound of it and asked the Queen if he could have that instead."
